entities.name: John of Crema
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
John of Crema was an Italian papal legate and cardinal, appointed by Pope Callistus II in 1121. This appointment marked a significant moment in the reform of the Catholic Church, as it brought John into the inner circle of the papacy and solidified his influence in the Church's governance.

As a cardinal, John of Crema played a crucial role in the Second Crusade, supporting the efforts of Emperor Lothair III and King Louis VI of France to reclaim the Holy Land from Muslim rule. The Crusade, which took place from 1147 to 1149, was a major turning point in the history of the Church and the Mediterranean region.

John of Crema's legacy can be seen in the subsequent reforms of the Church, particularly the establishment of the Inquisition in 1233, which aimed to root out heresy and ensure orthodoxy. His influence also extended to the Italian city-states, where he played a key role in the development of the papal-state's administrative structures.

In the words of his contemporary, the historian and theologian, Guibert of Nogent, 'John of Crema was a man of great piety, wisdom, and integrity, who served the Church with dedication and distinction.'
